meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everyone thinks of changing the world, but no one thinks of changing himself'?
meta.ogDescription: Tolstoy really did argue this in 1900 — but the famous wording isn't his. It's a later paraphrase, first traced to a 1999 book.

answer.label: Tolstoy’s idea — not his exact words
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment is genuinely Tolstoy’s, from “Three Methods of Reform” in Pamphlets: Translated from the Russian ↗ (1900, translated by Aylmer Maude) — but his actual wording is “everybody thinks of changing humanity, and nobody thinks of changing himself,” not the tidier “Everyone thinks of changing the world…” version that circulates online. Wikiquote ↗ traces that shorter phrasing to a 1999 book, not to Tolstoy.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Aylmer Maude, for the Free Age Press, 1900

source.excerpt: There can be only one permanent revolution — a moral one; the regeneration of the inner man. How is this revolution to take place? Nobody knows how it will take place in humanity, but every man feels it clearly in himself. And yet in our world everybody thinks of changing humanity, and nobody thinks of changing himself.
trail: Tolstoy wrote this passage in “Three Methods of Reform,” part of Some Social Remedies in his 1900 pamphlet collection, translated by Aylmer Maude for the pacifist Free Age Press ↗.

The Maude translation reads “everybody thinks of changing humanity, and nobody thinks of changing himself” — close in meaning to the popular quote, but not identical in wording, as confirmed in the full chapter text ↗.

Wikiquote ↗ lists “Everyone thinks of changing the world, but no one thinks of changing himself” as a variant, citing its earliest known appearance as The Artist’s Way at Work (1999) by Mark A. Bryan, Julia Cameron, and Catherine Allen — not any Tolstoy edition.
A scan of the original 1900 Free Age Press edition ↗ is on the Internet Archive.
source.excerptNote: This is Tolstoy’s own wording, in the 1900 Aylmer Maude translation — not the shorter “Everyone thinks of changing the world…” phrasing that circulates today.

source.rightsNote: The excerpt above is Aylmer Maude’s 1900 English translation, published well before 1931, so it is in the public domain. The shorter, more famous paraphrase in wide circulation online is a different matter — it doesn’t appear in this translation, and its own origin (traced by Wikiquote to a 1999 book) hasn’t been independently confirmed here.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.heading: About Leo Tolstoy
author.bio: Leo Tolstoy is best known for the novels War and Peace and Anna Karenina, but in his later decades he became a fierce moral and social critic, developing the Christian-anarchist philosophy of nonviolent resistance that later influenced Gandhi. Much of his later writing, distributed through the pacifist Free Age Press, argued that lasting social change had to begin with individual moral transformation.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The tidy, quotable “Everyone thinks of changing the world, but no one thinks of changing himself” is everywhere online as a direct Tolstoy quotation — but it doesn’t match what he actually wrote.

items.who: Quote sites (Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes, and others)
items.why: Present the short, punchy phrasing as a verbatim Tolstoy quotation with no citation to a specific work, when his actual 1900 translated sentence reads differently.
Wikiquote traces the familiar short wording to this book by Mark A. Bryan, Julia Cameron, and Catherine Allen, not to any translation of Tolstoy’s own writing, as shown on Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: What Tolstoy actually wrote, in Aylmer Maude’s 1900 translation of “Three Methods of Reform,” is: “And yet in our world everybody thinks of changing humanity, and nobody thinks of changing himself” — see the full text on Wikisource ↗.

context.heading: Where the real line comes from
lead: “Three Methods of Reform” is a short essay from Some Social Remedies, part of the pamphlet collection Tolstoy’s follower Vladimir Chertkov distributed through the Free Age Press in 1900. In it, Tolstoy weighs three ways reformers had proposed to relieve the condition of laborers, and argues that only a moral change beginning within each person can produce what he calls a “permanent revolution.”

That argument was one of the seeds of the Christian pacifism Tolstoy preached in his later decades, which went on to shape Gandhi’s thinking on nonviolent resistance. The line about everyone wanting to change humanity while no one changes himself was his summary of why, in his view, reform movements aimed outward kept failing.
